Resolved that it is expedient to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act, and to provide:
1.	That no duty shall be leviable on the value of any pension or portion thereof which is receivable as taxable income within the meaning of the Income War Tax Act.
Would the minister explain this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is to implement a recommendation of the Ives commission. At the present time a widow of a civil servant-I am taking this simply by way of- illustration

CMr. Dsley.l
who is entitled to a pension on the death of her husband under the superannuation act must pay succession duties on the commuted value of her pension, and then she pays an income tax on each annual pension payment. It was considered that in certain circumstances that was harsh, and the Ives commission made the recommendation that if income tax was payable on amounts paid under an^ pension scheme such as the superannuation act, the widow should not be obliged to pay succession duties as well. I refer to this only as a typical case; it is not confined, of course, to civil servants or to the superannuation scheme, but applies also to others.

Soldiers' pensions are
exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Soldiers' disability pensions are exempt from income tax, but I do not know of any exemption from succession duty of the commuted value of a disability pension. I think it is never large enough for that.
Would they come under this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not under this, because this applies only to pensions which are taxable income within the meaning of the Income War Tax Act.

Suppose a man buys six months prior to his death an annuity for a fairly large sum, say $100,000. If .he had willed that $100,000 to his family it would be subject to succession duty. By virtue of this proposed resolution will the $100,000 which was used to purchase an annuity under these circumstances be free from succession duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This resolution does not cover a case of the kind-, which, as the hon. gentleman has described it, is covered by our proposed legislation regarding the purchase of annuities. The taxation will be on the interest element alone.
Is that capital of $100,000 which is used to purchase an annuity a short time before the purchaser's death free from succession duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. One would have to look at the act and see whether it is a succession or not.
That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a difficult question to answer. A man buys an annuity, we will say. He does not know that he is going to die in six months' time. Suppose he lives fifteen years and the annuity has a guaranteed life of twenty years.

Succession Duty
I am referring to an annuity certain for fifteen or twenty years, payable to the estate or to the widow.

The point I am doubtful about, and I would have to get some information on this before answering, is whether if he dies within three years that is not a succession. Ordinarily if a husband makes a transfer to his wife or to anybody else within three years before he dies, it is regarded as passing to her on his death. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and I am very much obliged to my hon. friend for bringing up that point. If a man can do it, I want to know it too. I will give consideration to the matter before the bill comes in. You are a young man yet. You have lots of time.

speechtext: Really, just the words "taxable income" struck me as I read the section, and I wanted to get it cleared up. The minister mentioned the matter of estates of men who were killed in the war or died as a result of wounds received in the war. I should like to know what the situation is as to succession duties on those estates. In this connection the Canadian Legion passed a resolution at one of their meetings held in 1944 which reads as follows:
Be it resolved that we strongly urge the federal government to so amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act as to provide remission of
Succession Duty

succession duties for deceased members of the armed forces who died on active service or within one year of discharge.
The general opinion seems to be that the provinces are more generous in respect of these succession duty charges than the federal government is. As a matter of fact I received a letter the other day with reference to succession duties on the estate of a young man who was killed overseas and left his estate to his mother. I quote:
Estates of unmarried men who were killed in the forces, where the estate is over $5,000, are payable to the mother of the deceased. The province of Ontario, generally speaking, give consent so that the assets may be dealt with. As far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned if the estate is over $5,000 and if payable, as I have said above, to the mother there is no special consideration.
It went on to s'ay:
In my opinion there should be. If a boy gives his life for his country and has a little over $5,000 which is left for the benefit of the mother, I do not think the nation should tax this sum. My opinion is that up to $10,000 should be tax free under the conditions I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is very clearly set out, I may tell the hon. member, in section 7, subsection 3 of the Dominion Succession Duty Act. This section reads as follows:
(3) (a) Where the deceased dies from woumjs inflicted, accident occurring, or disease contracted while Canada is or was at war, and while on service with Canadian or any other of His Majesty's naval, military or air forces or with allied or associated naval, military or air forces, and where the Canadian pension commission finds that the circumstances are such that the widow or children of the deceased are entitled, or would, if such service had been with the Canadian naval, military or air forces, have been entitled to receive a pension under the Pension Act in respect of such death, or where the Canadian pension commission finds that the deceased died from wounds inflicted, accident occurring, or disease contracted, as a result of enemy action within twelve months before death;
(i)	the exemptions allowed in paragraphs
(a), (b) and (c) of subsection one of this section shall be increased by fifty per centum; and
(ii)	the amount of the duty payable in respect of a succession by any successor coming with class A or class B in the first schedule to this act shall be reduced to such sum as would, if accumulated at compound interest at the rate of three per centum per annum from the date of death with half-yearly rests, at the expiration of the period of the normal expectation of life of a person of the age of the deceased at the time of death (calculated in accordance with mortality tables approved by the minister), amount to the duty otherwise payable.
(b)	The Canadian pension commission shall on the request of the commissioner investigate the circumstances and report its findings in respect of any case arising under paragraph (a) of this subsectipn.

I would refer the hon. gentleman to a very considerable debate on this section, which the hon. member for Vancouver South will remember, and which took place in the summer of 1941 when we passed the Dominion Succession Duty Act.
Have there been any amendments since then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There have been no amendments. It does not grant complete exemption, but it grants a very considerable exemption.

I believe that in the budget debate last year the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough asked the minister to give consideration to the soldiers' insurance which men coming back from overseas are taking out to-day, and he asked that it should be excluded from any computation of succession duties. If I remember the discussion at that time, the minister seemed very favourably disposed to the suggestion and said he would look into it further. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no recollection of it: I am sorry. It may have been my parliamentary assistant.

speechtext: I do not understand how anything could depend upon the age of the widow.

Yes; it is payable on an annuity basis, and $9,006 will bring a pretty fair annuity. Under the government's system of assessing annuities or succession duties they would assess a pretty high value on a $10,000 policy.

I will look into the question.
I am sorry, but I do not seem to remember anything about it at all.

It was brought up in the last, budget debate.

Succession Duty

speechtext: My officials do not remember about it either.
I saw it the other day.

When an estate pays a succession duty on funds or property held in the United States does it also have to pay on the same amount in Canada?

Just so that we shall get this thing clear, does the Minister of National Revenue answer my question? Does he want the country to know now that it is the duty of the citizens of this country to give the names and addresses of those people or firms that they believe are evading payment of taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I think I can answer in the affirmative to that, that the department and the government, although they do not want the ordinary individual to be a "spotter" -as they are called-on anybody else, believe that it is in the interests of every individual who is paying income tax, and in the interests of the state, that those who are taxable should be called upon to make a return. I may tell the hon. member that I do not think there are many who are missed, or very many evasions, because the country is divided into regions, and the regional officers through the inspectors, who go to different communities, usually catch up with anybody in a community who has not put in a return. For instance, an inspector from the district of Ottawa will go to one of the Ottawa valley towns. He knows everybody there who is paying, and as he goes through that town, if it strikes him that the proprietor of a certain place of business, or certain individuals who are interlocked in the business activities of the community, have not made a return, he will very soon catch up with them. The number of people who should make returns and do not make them is almost a negligible quantity. But I repeat that if a citizen knows of people who are not paying their due amounts of taxes, I regard it as the duty of that citizen to acquaint the Department of National Revenue with the fact, and I assure you that those people will get the opportunity and the demand to make an income tax return, whether or not they are taxable.

I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue a question I asked a little while ago, with respect to the attempt which is being made to collect arrears of income tax from farmers. I am not objecting to the collecting of arrears of taxes from anybody, but I wish to bring to
December i, 1945
Supply-Post Office
the minister's attention a certain situation which the organized farmers have presented to me with the request that I bring it to his notice. It is represented that for several years after the thirties the farmers had to put up with worn-out machinery and depletion of their capital equipment1, and then after the war broke out they had great difficulty, when they began to get in better condition, in buying the machinery they wanted, and naturally so, because there was a real shortage. The result is that now, or as soon as they have an opportunity, they will make up the capital investment which they should have been making during those years, and meanwhile taxes will be placed on all that income which in reality ought to be capital. They are urging that a reprieve of five years from this form of'taxation is needed to give the farmers an opportunity to recover their economic position. I should like to know what the minister's view is of that representation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Perhaps I am not in a position to make the hon. member an answer which he would care to accept at this particular time. I will say that the representations he has made will be taken into consideration. But I can readily see many of the difficulties. If one class in the community asked for a remission of taxes for five years it would open up an avenue leading to all types of difficulties. I appreciate the difficulties the farmers have had; in this house in the last day or so the whole question of returns to farmers and fishermen has been discussed and the suggestion has been made that their returns might be placed on what one would call an average basis over a few years. That, together with the representations made by hon. gentlemen, will be taken into consideration with a view to dealing with all classes of the community in a spirit of justice and equity.

On that point I would ask the minister whether the same system of revenue collecting is followed in all parts of Canada. I believe there is an office in each , province. I am a little at sea about the last question raised. The officials in the province from which I come have done an efficient job of collection from the farmers in the past three years.
That goes for Saskatchewan.

I am speaking of those I know. The officials in my province have done a great deal to cooperate and have gone to every municipal office and obtained the record of the people. They have called them
in and made collections for the past two' or three years and I do not see how anyone could be missed. I was wondering if the same system is followed throughout Canada.
Mr. McCANN.: The system is absolutely uniform, the purpose being to treat all alike.
Resolutions reported, read the second time and concurred in.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: 281. Departmental administration, $811,425.

A few years ago in the city of Toronto, in, my own end of the city and I suppose in other parts as well, we had two deliveries of mail a day. Now we have only one. When are we to return to normal? If I posted a letter in Toronto on Friday night to myself I would not get it until Monday morning, but I would get it on Saturday afternoon if we had a normal delivery.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: This matter is under consideration. We still have over 1,100 employees with the forces and we need 390 more men to reestablish two deliveries a day.
In Toronto alone?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: In all Canada. That does not seem very much for all Canada, but it does not take twice as many men as we have now to reestablish two deliveries a day, because the run is shorter when there are two deliveries. We expect to be able to have two deliveries shortly. Some time next spring there will be two.

The postal employees, in my opinion, are as hard worked as any servants of the government. Certainly there are no employees who work harder than these men. They have long hours, and the mailmen carry heavy loads in all sorts of weather. I have observed them on my own street in Toronto and, whatever the reason is, their -work seems to play them out more quickly than others. [DOT] Too many of them have to retire because of hard work and long hours. I think they are poorly paid-I am speaking of the men who deliver the mails. Their job is a most important one, because the letters they deliver are sometimes priceless to those who receive them; yet you rarely hear of any misdeliveries or any mail troubles in this country. I for one am proud of the men in the postal service of Canada.

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It is well organized.

I do not know what the minister means by being well organized. If he is speaking of the staff, yes. I was not thinking of organization from the labour point of view because these men do not cause any trouble. They keep right on with their work. They never threaten to quit or to go on strike. I do not know what we would do if we did have such a strike. I hope the time is coming when the government will consider increasing the remuneration paid to postal employees and will also provide better working conditions. Some post offices furnish satisfactory conditions but many do not. In many the men are sorting down in the basement of some store or building in which they work. The government should make every effort to see that their working conditions are the best. Do they get two or three weeks' holiday in the summer?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Three weeks.
That is fair. Do they get paid during that time?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.
That is as it should be. With improved conditions, if they receive greater remuneration I have nothing more to say.

This is the first time the minister has appeared before the committee in his new capacity as Postmaster General, and I take this opportunity of expressing the hope that he will be happy in his new responsibilities. The members of this group are very much interested in his administration. We frequently refer to it as one impressive demonstration of what can be done under-
Public monopoly.
-government administration,-	_
Public monopoly is a misnomer.

-where the principle of free enterprise and competition has not been a factor. My hon. friends to the right have never suggested that the government should go out of this important service and turn it over to free enterprise to see how they would make out.
I could say a lot in a few words on that suggestion.

I think we have had a practical demonstration of what can be done under social planning where the greatest good

to the greatest number is concerned. I understand there have been some changes in the staff of the department, and I wonder if the minister would tell us who is now the deputy postmaster general, who is the assistant deputy, and what has become of the previous assistant deputy postmaster general.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We in fact have been paid a great compliment by a foreign country. Recently the republic of Peru entered into communication with my department asking us to send one of our officials in order to improve their postal system. We had a gentleman, Mr. Coolican, who was on the verge of reaching the age of superannuation, whom we asked if he would like to go to Peru for a few years. Mr. Coolican has accepted,, and the government has also accepted. The same thing has been done in regard to another official of the Canadian government in the Department of Public Works, whose services have been requested to improve the telephone and telegraph systems of that country. We have sent Mr. Sims to undertake that task. So that Mr. Coolican is now on leave, but he is the only high official who has left the department for some time. There are a few who have almost attained the superannuation age, and there may be some sort of reorganization in the near future, but at this time I could not say very much about that.
I was wondering if Mr. Coolican will be returning to the department or if he has retired.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: He has now gone to Peru in order to make definite arrangements with the government of that country. I do not know whether he is going to return. He was quite prepared to go there and help the government of Peru, and I am quite sure he will stay there for some time.
Is he not over age now?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: He has had one extension.

In view of what has been said by hon. members to my left about, this socialistic department and their experiences, I wish to ask the minister a question. I am hesitant about raising local problems on the floor of the house, but in my constituency I have a situation which is baffling to me and perhaps the minister could clear it up by stating his general policy in connection with the construction of post offices. I am quite aware that the Department of Public Works actually constructs or lets the contracts for these buildings, but I understand that is done on the recommendation of the Postmaster

Supply-Post Office
General. All during the war I have hesitated to bring up this matter, but according to the information I have received from responsible officials, in the instance I have in mind the government bought an old property and an adjoining property-with the intention of constructing a new post office just prior to the war. I am not sure what amount was paid for the property, but it is a matter of principle anyway. Ever since then the department has been paying the same people quite a nice monthly rent for the property, and I should like to understand why this has been done.
As I said, I realized that it would be unfair to say anything about the matter during the war years, but now that the war is over, these people are becoming agitated, and they think I should do- something about this on their behalf. The building is quite dilapidated; it is embarrassing to the officials of this town of about 1,200; it is an eyesore on the main street, and because it is crown property they are unable to tax it. They believe they should have a new post office now that the war is over. I understand that there is some policy followed by the department under which new post office buildings are not constructed unless there is a net revenue of something like S 10,000, but I should like to know from the minister just what the policy is, in fairness to these people who were content to stay quiet about the matter all during the war years but who consider they now deserve some reasonable explanation in regard to this unusual situation.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
It is true
that during the war the Department of Public Works was not called upon to construct any buildings for the Post Office Department, but we have had a survey made and intend to go ahead with quite a large number of buildings as soon as conditions permit. We do not want to enter into competition with the housing programme at this time, but we have definite plans to build quite a large number of post offices when the time comes. For a long time a rule has been established in the department that we put up public buildings in places where the net revenue is over $10,000, as the hon. member has said, and I must admit that in quite a few places where the revenue to-day is more than this amount they have not yet got their buildings, but we hope to be able to construct these buildings as soon as conditions permit.

I hope the minister will keep in mind the fact that his department is still paying rent on the property which belongs to it. I do not know what the argument in support of this may be, but to me
it is an unusual case. In view of that fact I think some exception might be made in this case. I should be glad if later on the minister would give some explanation of this unusual situation.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I am not
familiar with this particular case, but we do intend to commence the construction of these buildings as soon as possible.

I should like to ask the minister if we may soon expect the opening of postal service between Canada and the various camps in the British, United States and French occupied zones. I noticed an item in the New York Times under date of November 24, 1945, which stated:
Opening of a limited mail service for exchange of personal correspondence between Americans and displaced persons in the United States zones of Austria and Germany was announced to-day.
The state department, making the announcement, said it would also be possible to send five-pound gift parcels from this country to displaced persons in those zones.
The announcement said that in the interest of efficiency, it would be necessary that the first dispatch of mail originate in every case with the displaced person. Special postcard forms are being distributed in the American zones for this purpose.
Americans wishing to carry on the correspondence must present these cards before United States post offices will accept letters or parcels for mailing.
My question is, would it not be advisable for the minister to get in touch with the Department of External Affairs, and also to consult his own officials and endeavour to formulate a similar policy for the reestablishment of this postal service on the part of Canada. I should like to mention also that there are many Canadians who, particularly at this time, are interested in their own relatives who find themselves in these displaced persons' camps, and who certainly would be anxious to assist such people by sending parcels of food, clothing, medical supplies and so on. At the same time they are most anxious to correspond with their relatives as soon as this service is made available. Since the United States has been able to reopen the service I believe Canada should not lag far behind in following that good example.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We are in communication with the intermediary countries, and expect to be able to make an announcement any day now. We will do so as soon as we have reached an arrangement.

Would the minister give the committee details as to revenue from the Post Office Department which has been turned over to the treasury in the past year?
Supply-Post Office .

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I had intended to say a few words at the beginning. However, at this time I shall point out that in 1944-45 the net revenue was $66,055,519, and the net surplus, $13,097,000.
That is, more than $13 million has been turned over to the treasury as surplus.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.

Our custom has been to have a discussion when we deal with the first item. May I say to the minister that, from my limited acquaintance, I regard him very kindly indeed. I should also like to join in the complimentary remarks which have been made by hon. members to my left, but I find that I should make some further observations in view of what I have said about public monopolies. What I said was not said offensively, because this is one place where I agree that there is possibly good reason for a public monopoly. If it were handled in the manner for which my good friends would have you believe I have a preference, namely by private enterprise, it would be a very much muddled system. This is one instance where one can say that public enterprise is the most effective. I should like to emphasize, however, that, even here, there must be a degree of cooperation with private enterprise. Many of our common carriers, both air and rail, enter into this public service provided by the post office, and are doing a first-class job. Further, I can think of a score of smaller post offices owned by private individuals, where space is rented to provide this public service.
While the post office has been more or less a profitable venture-and perhaps I should use the word "service" rather than "venture"-because it- is bringing in a considerable amount of revenue to the public treasury, nevertheless the fact remains that with post office buildings as with other government buildings in- almost every locality, no taxes are being paid. Therefore it is hard to assess or to determine exactly the degree 3f efficiency of this organization, when one compares what it does with what private enterprise is required to do.
When I discovered the other day that the Department of Agriculture was paying $2,560 a year rental for 300 acres of land, I did not hear a shout from the other side of the house to the effect that this property should be owned by the people. I felt that it should.
I should like to know from the minister if at this time of the year postmen are receiving overtime pay.
[Mr. McKay.)

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.

The men who are delivering the mail on the many routes in the towns and cities, or wherever service is provided, are performing a tremendously long and laborious job. During the past number of years I know that our postman, in the process of his afternoon route, did not arrive at our home until around ten o'clock at night. Probably he would have a boy with him, pulling a sleigh laden with bags and parcels.
I join with the hon. member for Davenport in paying a real word of tribute to this' faithful army of men who are doing a remarkably fine job and are certainly not overpaid. I have always hesitated to' say too much about pay, because hon. members on this side of the house particularly, it seems to me, are always critical of expenditures made by the government, and I do not see how we can be consistent if in this instance we say, "You should pay more." I will, however, go so far as to say, that this is a group of men who are not overpaid and who have earned the admiration of all.
They are underpaid.
I hope they are receiving consideration for the extra long hours they must put in at certain seasons of the year.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: They receive extra pay for that.

I have a number of complaints from my constituents in the districts of Breton, Lindale and Berrymore. They are isolated districts, and at present they have only one mail delivery a week. These people enjoy few conveniences and would be most thankful if the minister could see his way clear to give them two mails a week instead of the one they are now getting. Will the minister look into this matter?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I shall, with pleasure.

I should like to say a word respecting another group in the postal service, who, I believe, are not overpaid. I refer to those who carry out the rural mail delivery. Probably they are the most underpaid group in the service, despite the fact that they render a real service to the Canadian rural population. Although there may have been some increases in pay. I believe they are still being paid a fairly low stipend.
I should like now to call the minister's attention to the necessity for the establishment of more rural mail delivery routes in western Canada. If one would travel through the

Supply-Post Office
west he would find that, in comparison with the east, we have comparatively little in the way of rural mail delivery. I realize, of course, that there are difficulties in that part of the country, because of our people being scattered. However, I notice that the department has a surplus of more than $13 million, and while during the war we have not urged that this service be extended, I consider that we are now justified in asking for an extension at as early a day as possible.
The rural routes in western Canada with which I am familiar have only two deliveries a week. There, again, improvement could be made by giving three deliveries on such routes. This would mean a great convenience to the people out there.
I should like to bring one further matter to the minister's attention. I have been told that quite recently the department issued regulations respecting the closing of all post offices on Sunday. I have had notification from my own constituents to the effect that certain post offices in that locality which formerly remained open for one hour on Sunday are now closed. In certain areas it happens that Saturday's mail does not arrive until after ten o'clock on Saturday evening, when the post offices in those areas are closed. The train leaves on Monday morning, with the result that business men are not able to answer their mail arriving on Saturday until Tuesday. This condition would be relieved if the post offices were left open for one hour on Sunday.
I leave these points for the minister's consideration.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We have
given the war-time bonus to mail carriers, and a little later on we gave also the cost of operation bonus. We have discovered that some of these contract rates are quite low. In many cases we are asking for new tenders and there will likely be a larger drain on the treasury, I said that in 1944-45 our net surplus was $13 million, but it must be remembered that that was a war year and we do not expect to be able to have the same surplus in the future. I shall consider what the hon. gentleman has said, and I wish he would send me details about those places where he wants three deliveries a week because I should like to refer that to the superintendent of the postal district. If we can do it, we shall be glad to do it. I wish to emphasize that this is not a revenue department; it is a service department.

There are some matters in my constituency which are somewhat at variance with the statement the minister made
earlier. First of all, I wish to refer to the retirement age of permanent and temporary employees of the Post Office Department. I understand that that age limit was waived during the war.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That is right.

The result is that in Regina- and I imagine the same is true of other places-there are a number of employees who should be given the opportunity to resign in order to make way for younger employees returning from overseas and elsewhere. In our city a number of requests have been received from returned persons to be taken on the post office staffs, and many of them have had to be refused.
Another problem is that cpnceming temporary employees. This relates not only to the Post Office Department but to all departments. The government policy of hiring persons requires serious revision. Temporary employees should be made permanent after a fixed period of employment, regardless of whether they are on an establishment or not. I have one specific case in mind which would come under the minister's department. This man has been employed by the Post Office Department in Regina for 23i years, having joined shortly after the last war. He is now 63i years of age, or li years from the usual retirement age. He was a veteran of the South African and the first world wars, and had two sons in the services during this war, one of whom was drowned in the North sea when his ship crashed.
This man wrote a civil service examination before being taken on the staff and he thought he had qualified for permanent employment. He has been permanently employed in the sense that he has not missed work in 23i years, but he is considered to be a temporary civil servant. He is now in poor health and is ready to retire. He has been thrifty, and I am sure he would not want me to mention his case on the floor of this house. He has never brought it up by way of complaint, but the fact is that he has no pension rights because he was not allowed to pay into the superannuation fund.
I am sure this case could be multiplied thousands of times in the government service. When a person is taken into the civil service and works for a period of five years or so without having been placed in a permanent establishment, he should be automatically classified as a permanent civil servant. I should like to know how this is handled in the minister's department.
I have a further request to make, one which was received just this morning. There are a
Supply-Post Office

number of veterans in Regina who would like to be reabsorbed into the Post Office Department. I urge that there be two deliveries daily in Regina so that these men may be taken into the employment stream. Then, with the retirement of the men and women who are sixty-five years of age or over there would 'be an added possibility of employment in that city. The minister said that there were too many postal employees still in uniform to permit the inauguration of two services daily, but I think by the time we retire the older employees we should be able to function with two services daily.
Then there is the matter of the revision of the wage schedule which would apply to the Post Office Department as well as to all branches of the civil service. I am glad that for once hon. gentlemen to my right and I can agree that it is time that we raised the salaries of civil servants. Would the minister care to make a statement at this time about the retirement age and making permanent those civil servants who have worked for a few years without being placed in a regular establishment?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: During the war employees were not retired at retiring age because of shortage of manpower, but our policy now is to retire them as soon as they reach the age of sixty-five years in order to give younger men a chance to be promoted.
Is that an automatic arrangement?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes. ,
Is their retirement at sixty-five years regardless of whether they have pensions?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: If they are employees of the Post Office Department they would be under the superannuation scheme and have a pension at sixty-five years. There may be some employees who are employed in what are known as revenue post offices. In these offices the postmaster gets a percentage of the revenue. Such employees would not be under the superannuation system. Previously they were not retired at sixty-five years. They might be postmasters in villages or small towns and were kept on as long as they were able to do their work properly, but in the near future it is our intention to ask them to retire at sixty-five years.

Would the minister give the committee some indication of what security these people are to have, or are we just going to turn them out like an old work-horse to rough it on the prairie and support themselves as best they can?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
These men have a contract with the government under which they receive a certain percentage of the revenue, and in some places more than the revenue. But we have a minimum. There are small post offices where the revenue is not half the amount that we are paying to the postmaster. As I said before, this is a service department, not a department for revenue. Most of these men have some other job besides running the post office, which is very often looked after by the son or the daughter or the wife. Like anybody else working on a contract with anybody they must look to their own future. Of course ' there is the old age pension which begins at a certain age, but there is no machinery established to-day, just for the Post Office Department, to superannuate these postmasters when they leave at sixty-five years of age.
The hon. member also asked about temporary employees, and I am in great sympathy with what he said. But especially during the war every employee that we have taken on has had to sign a document clearly explaining that he was only working in a temporary capacity in order that we might keep the position open for a returned man.
As to the returned man who has been in the department before, he is taken on again immediately he presents himself. My hon. friend mentioned one employee who had been a temporary for twenty-three years. I do not quite understand how he has been with us so long as a temporary. I do not know just what we can do for him, but if the hon gentleman will give me the details I shall be very glad to see if we can do something for him if he is a veteran.
There was one other question, about reclassification of wages.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That question is being studied generally, not only in my department but in all departments. Of course the treasury board has something to say about that.

I have one general question that I wish to ask the Postmaster General, but before I do so I wish to comment briefly on one or two things that have been said in the discussion.
I was very glad to hear the Postmaster General say that something was being done to raise the remuneration of rural mail couriers. At every session of parliament that I can remember, for quite a number of years, this question has been discussed and demands have been made for increased remuneration for rural mail couriers, and if the Postmaster

Supply-Post Office
General has a general plan for improving their remuneration ! hope that when it comes before us the house will support him, because it is a reform, if that is the proper term, that is long overdue.
The hon. member for Grey North mentioned overtime for letter carriers. I did not refresh my memory before coming into the chamber, but my understanding is that the present system of overtime payment is very unsatisfactory, at least from the letter carrier's point of veiw, because I understand that overtime is not a matter of a cash payment but compensation in the form of holidays later on. I may be mistaken in that, but I do not think I am. I think the letter carriers have to take days off during the summer to compensate them for overtime work during the Christmas and New Year's rush.
The question of temporary civil servants raised by the hon. member for Regina City, as every hon. member knows who has been in the house very long, is an old one. In almost every department there are civil servants who have been there for years and are still temporaries. I do not think the one with twenty-three years temporary service is a particularly outstanding case, because I have heard of longer periods of temporary service than that. On the house staff the situation was corrected following recommendations made by a civil service committee some few years ago. It is a question that I think should be dealt with in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Regina City. That is, any person taken into the employ of the government in a permanent department should, after two years' service at most-I would not say five years because that is too long-become a permanent civil servant. The situation is quite different, of course, if the department itself is only a temporary one.
The question I was going to ask the Postmaster General was, what is the method of printing and selling postage stamps? Does the government purchase stamps; where are they printed, and how are they sold? In the larger post offices such as Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal, are the stamps sold on a commission?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: In normal times the employee who works overtime is given time off to compensate him, but during the Christmas rush, which lasts for almost the whole of December and part of January, we pay for overtime.
At what rate?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: At the regular rate.
At the regular hourly rate or the regular overtime rate?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
At the regular hourly rate, and we give them time off. In the city of Toronto we take on almost 5,000 temporary employees just for the Christmas rush, and almost as many, if not more, in Montreal.
As to the stamps, we ask for tenders for the printing of the stamps. They are printed to-day and have been for some time by the Canadian Bank Note company, and by the way, our stamps are considered by philatelists as the best in the world. In the large post office the custom for many years has been to permit certain people to have the privilege of selling stamps on a commission. They have to employ and pay their own assistants, and they have to buy the stamps for cash. That system is in operation in a great number of the large post offices. In the smaller post offices we sell the stamps ourselves, and that practice has also been followed in some of the large cities where drug stores ano other stores have the privilege of selling stamps on a commission, but this practice is disappearing in the larger cities. In Toronto the department is selling its own stamps Wherever a man is doing his work properly and giving satisfaction to the public we dc not disturb him in his position, but when he dies or ceases to operate his franchise the department takes it over.

Would the minister give me some further information on that, if not now on some future day? Is that system of selling stamps on commission used in the general post office at Vancouver? Who is the contractor and what is the commission paid?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I have all the details here for every town and city, the number of employees and so forth.

I should like to know
the number of employees in the Vancouver post office, the rate of commission paid, the amount paid in commissions and the profit that the contractor is making.

Do the contractors
, include any wholesale merchants?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We have what we call lobby vendors selling stamps in the post office. We have not what might be termed wholesale vendors of stamps.

It is now over thirtj years since the rural mail service was set up It has been of great service to the rural people, who appreciate it very much, and I
Supply-Post Office

wish to pay my tr^oute to the rural mail couriers for the splendid work they are doing in good weather and bad the year round, going out in the storms of winter and making their way through snowbanks and over the fields to take the mail to the boxholders. It is over thirty years since that system was established, and I think a resurvey should be made of a good many of the rural routes with a view to giving more contract service to bring this convenience to more rural box-holders. I know of numerous instances where thirty years ago there was only a grass farm but where to-day there are houses and buddings, and yet the farmer has to walk three-quarters of a mile to a mile to get his mail. In western Ontario particularly, which I know better than any other part, a resurvey of the rural mail routes should be made to serve better the rural people in that part of the province.

I was quite interested to hear the hon. member for Mackenzie pay a tribute to the government for the example which the post office is of public enterprise, but of course there never has been anything else but government management of the post office. It is one department where there is absolutely no competition, and I do not think it is a just comparison because, if there were any competition, the post office picture might not look quite so rosy. Again, I do not know that we can be so proud of some of the post offices that we have to go into. I know the method which the minister has described, that some of the offices are what are known as revenue offices and some of the postmasters are revenue postmasters. They supply the best equipment they can and at the same time make a living, which means, of course, that some of the post offices are very dingy, some broken down, needing electric light bulbs so that we can see to write our name on an envelope, and lacking in other respects. I am quite certain that if there were any competition many of these post offices would not do very much business.
Since this is one department of government that is revenue producing, it is only natural that we can expect it to show an annual profit. This is one public enterprise that believes in the profit system, because it is producing a profit eveiy year; $19,000,000, I think the minister said wTas the surplus this year.
I would ask the minister when the country can expect a reduction in the postage rate now that the department has a $19,000,000 profit. Since there is no competition, all the government have to do is to boost the postage
TMr. McCubbin.]
rate and of course they would have a biggpr profit. If they lowered the rate too much they would have a loss. Just how many employees are there in the postal service in Canada, taking in everyone? The government might not have to raise their wages very much to use up that $19,000,000 surplus. There are a good many ways of looking at this matter of public enterprise.
I should like to refer to the mail couriers again. The phrase that they are out in the winter storms has been used by nearly every hon. member who has spoken, and I should also like to pay my tribute to these men. I do not know whether that is what they want to be paid. I think they want to be paid in cash.
That is what I advocated. We cannot blame them for that.

It will be very nice for
them to get Hansard and to read all the tributes we have been paying them. But what they want payment in is cash, not tributes. I am sure that the people of Canada are waiting to hear from the Postmaster-General about a reduction in the postage rate. Did I hear him say something, or was it just imagination?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I must correct a few misapprehensions. The Post Office Department cannot give a statement showing the net profit because like every other department our revenues are deposited in the consolidated revenue fund, and for the money we need we come before the house, as every other department must do, and ask in the estimates for the sum that is required to carry on for the next year. That gives the house an opportunity of checking everything that we are doing.
Not so late in the session; you cannot do so.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
If we were a company showing a statement, whether we have profits or not, we would have our money in the bank and might not in times like these have to come to the house and ask for a subsidy of $60,000,000 or something like that. We increased the postage during the war by one cent, which has brought to the government about $10,000,000 more in revenue. The department intends to ask for a reduction from the present rate and come back to two cents for drop letters and three cents for the others. Our aim is even higher, but I will not say exactly what it is in case my target is too high. We want as soon as possible to transport all our first-class mail

by plane from one end of Canada to the other so that, as far as the postal department is concerned, the dominion will be only twenty-four or thirty-six hours, or, at the utmost, forty-eight hours large, so to speak. That would be a great thing for the unity of the country. Of course we are waiting on the department administered by my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction to inform us when we shall be able to carry all first-class mail by plane.	.
Would that include the far north, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, I do not know if it is the intention of the committee to go through the different estimates, but if hon. members would like to go fast I may say that we are asking this year for over 810,000,000 for air mail services. Of course we are losing money on the operation, because it costs us more than it would if we were sending our mail by some other means, especially when we send it into the far north where planes carry very little except mail. We expect to be able to reduce the rate very soon both on land and in the air. We have 39,208 employees, including rural mail carriers. There are a large number of rural mail carriers and sometimes they work only part of the day, but that is the number of employees we have. There are 1,098 at headquarters in Ottawa and we still have 1,651 who are with the army. As a matter of fact, the number is really eleven hundred and something but when this figure was prepared it was 1,651.
Why not give the committee a report on the quantity of air mail carried?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I could do that.

The hon. member for Peterborough West requested me last night to ask a question with regard to salaries paid to postal men. Apparently they were promised an increase of 8300 per annum, but instead of being given that increase-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is confusing what is promised with what is asked for.	.
This is what I am told. I understand that they were granted an increase of $120 a year, from $1,500 to $1,620, whereas they were led to believe that they would get an increase of $300.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It seems that I shall have to be the one questioning instead of being the one questioned. I do not know by whom they were promised S300.
They asked for it.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: They asked for $300 and were given $120.
Does the minister say that no such promise was given?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: There is no such promise, I am informed.

One other question. I am told that if a person uses the blue airmail form for delivery in Canada the letter is returned; it is not delivered, although the fee for that letter is ten cents, whereas for the ordinary airmail letter it is only seven. Why is that? There is nothing on the form itself to show that it is for use only for overseas. I suggest that if this blue form is to be used only for letters sent overseas a notation to that effect should be printed on it.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We abandoned the airgraph form in July of this year.
I do not mean the airgraph form but the blue form which is in use. I sent one overseas myself the other day.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: There must be some confusion, because we have no particular form of letters to-day for airmail in Canada, although we did have at the start. We were using a very light envelope. To-day businessmen use ordinary envelopes and letterheads for airmail and the fee is seven cents.

I am speaking of the blue form. A person can go into the post office and pick up one of these forms, and in fact that was done by the person who wrote to me. He did not send a letter overseas but posted one from Winnipeg to Vancouver. He paid ten cents postage and the letter was not delivered in Vancouver. After a long delay it was returned to the sender, and yet there is nothing on the form to show that it must be used only for overseas.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I shall make inquiries concerning the matter.
I wish to bring up a couple of matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.
